data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is true or probable, but as a critical-rational decision rule: acting on the theory that has withstood the severest tests maximizes the exposure of error should the theory be false, thereby adhering to the methodological imperative of falsificationism even in practical application.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the chosen theory fails, the collapse must yield a clearer, more severe falsification than any alternative would have provided.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The preference must be explicitly framed as a convention for maximizing learning potential, not as a belief in future success probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The agent must remain willing to abandon the theory immediately upon any contrary evidence, treating the action itself as a test.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical-Rational Decision Rule: The agent selects the hypothesis that offers the highest 'potential falsifiability' given current evidence. By choosing the best-corroborated theory (the one surviving the toughest attempts at refutation), the agent ensures that if their action leads to failure (e.g., a bridge collapses), the resulting falsification will be most informative and severe. This converts practical action into a continuation of the testing process rather than a retreat into induction.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
